\section{Bias Identity Validation with Real Confusion Matrices}
\label{app:realcm_bias}

Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} is derived under symmetric misclassification (A2); real LLM confusion matrices are asymmetric (FPR $\neq$ FNR).
We verify that the generalized identity $\mathrm{bias}(z,s) = \Delta\tau \cdot [B_s]_{z,1}$ (Remark~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) holds under real annotation error structures by running semi-synthetic simulations ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K{=}4$, $\Delta\tau{=}0.30$, 100 MC runs) with confusion matrices drawn from 11 LLM--dataset combinations: eight models on TweetEval (GPT-4-turbo, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-3.5-turbo, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B) and three on Civil Comments (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-3.5-turbo).

Table~\ref{tab:realcm_r2} reports per-model $R^2$ from regressing observed subgroup bias on the predicted value $\Delta\tau \cdot [B_s]_{z,1}$.
The aggregate $R^2 = 0.975$; 10 of 11 combinations achieve $R^2 \geq 0.93$.
The single outlier (GPT-4o-mini on Civil Comments, $R^2{=}0.76$) has near-homogeneous subgroup error rates ($\max|[B_s]_{z,1}| = 0.089$), so predicted biases are small and Monte Carlo noise dominates the regression.
$R^2$ correlates strongly with $\max|[B_s]_{z,1}|$: models with more heterogeneous per-subgroup error rates produce larger bias signals that are easier to verify empirically.

12	We formalize this problem and derive an exact bias identity for the correction-induced error.
13	When a pooled confusion matrix is applied to correct subgroup CATEs, it misattributes error across subgroups with an exact product form: the bias in subgroup $s$ equals $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$, where $\delta_s$ is the deviation from the pooled error rate and $\Delta\tau$ is the CATE heterogeneity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}).
14	This is not a bound but an exact population-level identity, verified empirically with $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $R^2 = 0.974$ ($K{=}4$).
15	A direct consequence is that global correction can be worse than no correction at all: in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations (260/520) across our parameter grid, global correction increases absolute bias relative to the naive estimator, with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest).
